title: Reply Comments of Crusoe Energy Systems, Inc. re the Notice Inviting Comments and Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking under RM26-4.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                BEFORE THE
                  FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate                     Docket No. RM26-4-000
Transmission System

             REPLY COMMENTS OF CRUSOE ENERGY SYSTEMS, INC.

       Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (Commission) October 27,

2025 Notice Inviting Comments and the November 7, 2025 Notice Granting Extension of

Time, Crusoe Energy Systems, Inc. (Crusoe) submits these reply comments in support of the

Department of Energy’s (DOE) Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANOPR)

requesting that FERC establish standardized interconnection procedures and agreements for

large loads seeking to interconnect to the transmission system. 1

I.     SUMMARY OF COMMENTS

      Crusoe is a vertically integrated Artificial Intelligence (AI) infrastructure company that

builds, owns, and operates data centers specifically optimized for the high-performance

computing requirements of artificial intelligence and machine learning workloads. Crusoe's

primary operations involve sourcing and developing cost-effective energy, including natural

gas, intermittent renewable power (e.g., wind, solar) and battery storage, to power its data

center facilities. Crusoe leverages its in-house manufacturing capabilities to rapidly deploy

computing infrastructure that provides reliable, low-latency cloud services, including access to

leading-edge graphics processing units (GPUs), to enterprise customers and AI developers.




1
  Letter from DOE Secretary Wright to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (Oct. 23, 2025),
attaching the Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, Ensuring Timely and Orderly Interconnection
of Large Loads.
 Docket No. RM 26-4-000

Through its energy-first approach, Crusoe aims to reduce both the cost and the environmental

impact of utility-scale computing infrastructure.

      The proposed technical requirements discussed in the ANOPR could enable companies

like Crusoe that control both the build and design specifications of their facilities to serve as

effective early implementers of these enhanced interconnection standards. Crusoe is actively

contributing to the development of technical and policy frameworks across the country that

enhance grid reliability while accommodating flexible load operations.

      To prevent market inefficiencies, the Commission should establish heightened standards

for large load and hybrid facility interconnection requests, including a significant increase in

deposit fees and site control requirements to deter speculative requests. Additionally, large

load and hybrid facility interconnection customers must be required to demonstrate actual

technical capability and financial commitment, rather than securing queue positions based

solely on qualitative commitments that could impede legitimate development opportunities.

Without such safeguards, speculative queue positions could significantly disrupt AI computing

development by creating uncertainty around the transferability and value of interconnection

rights and potentially deterring investment in data center development.

      The Commission should also prioritize hybrid facilities that combine load

interconnection requests with onsite generation because they can reduce load requirements and

provide valuable generation support to the grid during peak demand. Hybrid facilities should

be studied based on the specific load withdrawal and generation injection rights requested and

be recognized as structures that cause significantly less impact to the transmission grid than

large loads that do not bring generation.




                                                 2
 Docket No. RM 26-4-000

        Finally, reforms are needed on the federal level to support the rapid deployment of AI

infrastructure. Coordinated federal action is needed to improve transmission construction and

equipment procurement timelines. In addition, the Commission should adopt Public Utility

Holding Company Act (PUHCA) regulation reforms to remove federal impediments to power

supply arrangements by eliminating “sleeve” power purchase agreement (PPA) requirements

where retail sales are allowed by states.

II.     REPLY COMMENTS

        A.      Reply Comments on the ANOPR’s Principles for Reform

                Principle 1: Large load and hybrid facility interconnection processes should
                be developed pursuant to federal jurisdiction.

        Large load and hybrid facility interconnections will have a significant impact on the

regional and interregional transmission grid across multiple states. Most commenters agree

that large load and hybrid facility interconnection processes should be developed pursuant to

federal jurisdiction to ensure relatively consistent rules apply across the country.

                Principle 2: Reforms should be applicable to new loads greater than 100
                MW.

        The proposed 20 MW threshold for the new large load and hybrid facility

interconnections may be too low to efficiently advance AI deployment. The Commission

should consider raising the threshold to facilities above 100 MW. 2 If the threshold is too low,

the queue will be bogged down with relatively small interconnections that would better be

served through existing load interconnection processes. To ensure that regulatory reforms

adequately support efforts to advance AI deployment, streamlined processes should prioritize

large facilities above 100 MW. For example, Crusoe has under development facilities in the

1,200 MW range with both grid interconnection and onsite natural gas production. Facilities of

this scale will accelerate AI deployment in the United States and should be prioritized through

interconnection reforms.

                Principle 3: Load and hybrid facilities should be studied together with
                generating facilities.
        Crusoe has revolutionized co-located generation and scaled the technology to enable

colocation to high levels currently deployed today. Consistent with this third principle, hybrid

facilities combining interconnection requests with onsite generation should be prioritized as

they can reduce load requirements while potentially supporting the grid during peak demand. 3

Joint interconnection studies for hybrid facilities that bring new generation with load will

expedite the interconnection process and minimize the need for costly and time-consuming

construction of network upgrades because the impact of the new load can be offset by the

addition of new generation.




too low” and a “100 MW nationwide threshold would be more appropriate than the ANOPR’s 20 MW
proposal.”).

                 Principle 4: Load and hybrid facility interconnection requests should be
                 subject to heightened standards to prevent speculative interconnection
                 requests from clogging the queue.

          Speculative interconnection requests are hindering AI deployment across the country.

Speculative requests will continue to delay interconnection for large scale projects and lead to

uncertainty in real load demand. In addition to causing delays in interconnecting non-

speculative load, speculative interconnection requests are problematic in a number of other

areas such as ensuring resource adequacy, transmission planning, and reliability.4 Crusoe

supports the comments of Google 5 and OpenAI 6 asking the Commission to impose heightened

standards for interconnection requests, including significant increase in deposit fees and site

control requirements to deter speculative requests. Heightened interconnection standards will

also provide transmission planners with more accurate information to expedite interconnection

studies and get a clearer picture of a new large load’s impact on the transmission system.

          Interconnection queue management and technical requirements must balance speed with

legitimacy. Crusoe supports the ANOPR's goal of significantly expediting interconnection

service for large loads. To do this, the Commission should seriously consider whether

managing an interconnection queue on a first-come, first-served serial (or cluster) basis will

achieve the goal of interconnecting large loads in an efficient and expedited manner. Serial

queues with low thresholds will not be workable. The Commission should instead establish

clear, objective criteria that require interconnection customers to demonstrate both technical

capability and financial commitment beyond mere qualitative assurances of curtailment

flexibility. Without such safeguards, speculative applicants could secure advantageous queue

positions without demonstrating actual technical ability to meet the enhanced performance

requirements, thereby creating barriers to entry for legitimate developers and introducing

significant uncertainty into project valuation and transferability.

        This dynamic would have particularly adverse consequences for the financial and

investment markets where the ability to conduct meaningful due diligence on the enforceability

and legitimacy of interconnection rights is essential to facilitating efficient capital deployment

in the data center and energy infrastructure sectors. Crusoe therefore urges the Commission to

develop robust qualification standards that balance the need for expedited processing with the

imperative of maintaining queue integrity and market confidence. Such qualification standards

can include site control requirements, 7 minimum queue fees of $100,000 or greater, and

tendering full security for transmission upgrades.

                Principle 5: Hybrid facilities should be studied based on the amount of
                injection or withdrawal rights.

        New large load and hybrid facility interconnection processes should study the specific

load withdrawal and generation injection rights requested by large load and hybrid facility

developers. Hybrid facility structures cause significantly less impact on the transmission grid

than large loads that do not bring generation. Thus, where hybrid facilities are proposed, the

 Options to purchase should be acceptable to demonstrate site control to enable developers to ensure

load and generation should be studied together to get an accurate picture of the load’s impact

on the grid. 8 The Commission should recognize that a one-size-fits-all study process that does

not distinguish between hybrid facilities and large loads will discourage innovative solutions to

expediting AI computing technologies.

        The Commission should follow ERCOT’s lead in exploring the feasibility of an

expedited study process for controllable load and generation to interconnect and economically

dispatch in the wholesale market and to participate as voluntary load shed resources. Hybrid

facilities should be viewed as flexible resources that can provide system-wide reliability

benefits while having a minimal impact on the transmission system.

        Finally, Crusoe supports SPP’s currently proposed High Impact Large Load (HILL) and

High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (HILLGA) model because it is proactive and

supported by a broad group of industry stakeholders. SPP’s model recognizes the need to

preserve grid-connected generation for resource adequacy and reliability concerns.

                Principle 6: Hybrid interconnections should be required to install
                protection facilities to prevent unauthorized injections or withdrawals.

        The Commission should require hybrid interconnections to install the system protection

facilities necessary to prevent unauthorized injections or withdrawals that exceed the respective

                Principle 7: Interconnection studies should be expedited for large loads that
                are curtailable and co-located generators that are dispatchable.

        Crusoe supports flexible interconnection rules that will streamline large load

interconnections for prioritized national projects. Specifically, Crusoe supports expedited

interconnection study procedures to prioritize proven flexible load technologies. As a leader in

flexible computing, Crusoe supports expedited processes as discussed by Emerald AI, 10

Google, 11 OpenAI, 12 and others. 13 However, it is critical that companies must demonstrate

actual technical ability to curtail loads and advance flexible computing to be eligible for

expedited interconnection. If there are no stringent requirements for flexible load, the

Commission could inadvertently create inefficiencies if unproven technologies are prioritized

and expedited. By offering expedited interconnection schedules for demonstrated flexible load,

the Commission will encourage innovative solutions to ensure flexible load can perform as

expected. For example, any AI computing facility can become a fully flexible load by

switching to their own 100% back up power source, including a natural gas plant or by pairing

wind or solar with batteries.

        Once in the study process, subsequent rule or process changes should not apply to

pending interconnection requests retroactively. Crusoe is concerned that projects can get

caught in a never-ending spiral of rule changes that will cause considerable delays even for

projects that are nearly finished with the interconnection process. 14 Crusoe has been an

industry leader in developing new technology, such as voltage ride-through (VRT) capability

solutions, but such innovations have caused additional unforeseen delays in receiving approvals

to interconnect. New rules when applied retroactively will only cause delays and clog the

interconnection queues with the inevitable re-studies. Any new rules developed in this NOPR

process or thereafter should apply to new projects and should not move the goal posts for

projects already being processed under an earlier set of rules.

                Principles 8, 11 and 12: Load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for
                transmission and ancillary services costs that are fair and reasonable.

        Large loads and hybrid facilities should pay their fair share of current and future grid

costs based on their use of the grid. For load, that means the power that is withdrawn from the

grid, not what the load consumes in total.



14
   For example, Senate Bill 6 requires ERCOT to conduct additional studies for new large loads to co-
locate with existing generation resources, a requirement that is now delaying projects that were already
past the study process. See S.B. 6, 89th Leg. (Tex. 2025). In addition, ERCOT has identified voltage
ride through (VRT) capability difficulties, yet there are no standards that exist for measuring load VRT
capability. This is resulting in uncertainty and delay in the interconnection process.


                                                    9
 Docket No. RM 26-4-000

        Transmission and ancillary services charges should be assigned to hybrid facilities

based on the specific grid services that the load and generation uses. Under ERCOT’s

generation netting rules, for example, generation and load behind a shared interconnection are

netted together such that in each market settlement interval (fifteen minutes) if more power is

flowing out (net generation on the grid) then it is settled as generation and no grid charges

apply. If more power is flowing in during the interval (net load), then it is settled as load with

applicable grid charges. Large loads and hybrid facilities should thus pay their fair share of

current and future grid costs based on their use of the grid.

                Principle 9: Load and hybrid facility interconnection customers should
                have the option to build interconnection facilities and network upgrades.

        Load and hybrid facility interconnection customers should have the same option to

build interconnection facilities and network upgrades as currently provided to generator

interconnection customers. 15 In particular, co-located generation in a hybrid facility

interconnection structure is in a good position to expedite the construction of eligible upgrades.

                Principle 10: An existing generating facility that seeks to enter a partial
                suspension to serve a new load at the same location must go through a
                system support resource (SSR) or reliability must run type study.

        The Commission should first define what an “existing generator” is for purposes of the

necessary withdrawal studies. For example, an existing generator could be defined as any

generator that was operational as of January 1, 2026. That operational date should remain the

same and not become a moving target. Any generation installed after that date would not be

considered an existing generator that is subject to withdrawal studies.

       Any proposal to withdraw an existing generator from market availability should be

subject to a transmission security study and a resource adequacy study, with a defined timeline

for each. If operational problems are shown in the studies, RTOs should be able to impose

conditions on the withdrawing generator, such as giving the RTO the right to call back the

power to the grid when needed.

               Principle 13: There must be a plan to implement large load and hybrid
               interconnection reforms.

       Given the current data center demand, Crusoe supports the DOE Secretary’s request for

final Commission action by April 30, 2026. As noted above, any new rules developed should

not apply to interconnection requests retroactively. Any new rules developed in this

rulemaking process or thereafter should apply to new projects and should not move the goal

posts for projects already being processed under an earlier set of rules.

       B.      Other Needed Reforms to Support Rapid Deployment of AI Infrastructure.

               1.      Coordinated federal action is needed to improve transmission
                       construction and equipment procurement timelines.

      Crusoe commends the proposed ANOPR’s policy improvements to shorten study

timelines for large load and hybrid facility interconnections. That is one of the major sources

of delay in the deployment of AI computing infrastructure. Two other sources of delay are (1)

transmission inadequacy and construction timelines and (2) the long lead times for transmission

and generation equipment. While these sources of delay are not specifically addressed in the

ANOPR, it is imperative that federal policies step in to address these delays on a



                                                11
 Docket No. RM 26-4-000

comprehensive basis. For example, to address transmission construction delays and lack of

interregional planning, the Commission should be more aggressive in deploying its backstop

siting authority where needed.

      In addition, supply chain constraints for gas and electrical long lead equipment represent

a separate challenge that will require complementary policy solutions. Even with expedited

interconnection studies, the time required to manufacture, deliver, and energize network

upgrades and new transmission facilities will continue to create long lead times before large

loads can be energized. Currently, developers of transmission, generation and load

interconnections are all competing for the same equipment. Interconnections can require new,

custom-built transformers and voltage step-down equipment, which, in some cases, require up

to 48 months to procure. This procurement timeline effectively becomes the critical path for

project development, regardless of how fast the interconnection study process is conducted.

       Thus, to fully realize the benefits of expedited large load interconnection procedures,

the Commission and other federal agencies should work together to develop complementary

federal policy initiatives focused on domestic manufacturing capacity and production timelines

for electrical long lead equipment that could significantly enhance the rapid deployment of data

centers and other large loads. Strengthening the domestic supply chain for transformers,

switchgear, and other critical electrical equipment would not only accelerate large load

interconnection timelines but also enhance energy security and grid resilience more broadly.

               2.     The Commission should adopt PUHCA reforms to remove federal
                      impediments to power supply arrangements by eliminating “sleeve”
                      PPA requirements where retail sales are allowed by states.

      Crusoe supports EDF power solution, Inc.'s recommendations regarding reforms to the

Commission's Public Utility Holding Company Act (PUHCA) regulations that effectively



                                               12
 Docket No. RM 26-4-000

require independent power producers to enter into sleeve PPAs to maintain PUHCA

exemptions. 16 By requiring sleeve PPAs in states that would otherwise allow retail sales to

large loads, the PUHCA regulations create significant impediments to hybrid facility

development and increase costs. Sleeve requirements impose unnecessary transaction costs and

delays by requiring a regulatory "middleman" whose involvement adds no operational or

commercial value but is necessary solely to maintain PUHCA exemptions for upstream owners

and investors. Eliminating the sleeve requirement to maintain PUHCA exemptions for

upstream owners would reduce costs and accelerate project development.

III.   CONCLUSION

       For the foregoing reasons, Crusoe requests that the Commission proceed expeditiously

to develop interconnection rules that ensure the reliable and speedy interconnection of new

large loads and hybrid facilities of national importance.
